children: A block off Central Park, JPMorgan Chase is turning a 1930s three-story brick building into a new offering for its richest clients: an exclusive Upper East Side club.

JPMorgan has been renovating the mansion-like structure at the corner of Madison Avenue and East 64th Street — built as an elaborate bank branch by its predecessor, Bank of Manhattan — for more than a year to allow it to serve food and drink. Public filings show audacious plans to turn the space into something akin to a members club, complete with lounges and a dining room, kitchen and bar.

The space is likely to be used as a venue to host clients of its private bank, which provides white-glove service to its highest-end customers, people familiar with the matter said. To be a private-bank client at JPMorgan, a client needs at least $10 million in investable assets.
The exact programming for the space is still being determined, a spokesman said.
The endeavor, code-named Project Ruby, is the latest effort by JPMorgan to bolster its luxe spaces and services for wealthy clients.

The bank added to its wealth-management business locations when it acquired failed bank First Republic and upgraded many of its branches into JPMorgan-branded locations, complete with additional amenities like private offices and libraries. They are a step up from its Chase brand, which is the biggest consumer bank in the country.

JPMorgan Chase has been building airport lounges, acquired travel services to plan vacations and added new offerings for its well-to-do clients, including connecting them with vendors for anything from private jets to valuing art.

These ultrawealthy customers are at the center of a fight in the banking world in recent years. The banks earn significant fees for managing their fortunes, but are fighting to take on their entire financial lives: offering advice to their estates and to their businesses.

Surging stocks since the pandemic and explosive-artificial intelligence investments have left a large and growing pie of wealth held by the top 0.1% of Americans. Blockbuster initial public offerings of long-private companies, notably SpaceX and Anthropic, have minted millionaires overnight. A generation of baby boomers is both figuring out how to spend their wealth and how to pass it down.

Other wealth managers and credit-card companies have launched similar high-end services, and some have built clubs for clients. But an expansive private-event space would be a new arrow in JPMorgan's quiver for the ultrawealthy.

The neo-Georgian building was completed in 1933 at the height of the Great Depression as a branch for Bank of the Manhattan Trust Company, which would eventually merge into Chase and then JPMorgan. In recent years it has served as an old-fashioned Chase branch for modern-day JPMorgan Chase, complete with ATMs.

It is in an elite neighborhood, standing a few steps from a window display featuring paisley leather handbags of Italian luxury fashion house Etro; the Beretta Gallery, which prominently displays hunting jackets but none of its firearms; and De Beers diamond necklaces.

The bank expects costs for the project to be about $19 million, according to an analysis of city filings by The Wall Street Journal. Records show the bank is installing a new heating, ventilation and air conditioning system, plus an elevator and two dumbwaiters for kitchen service — all part of a near gut renovation of the historic structure.
Some details of Project Ruby were earlier reported by the lifestyle newsletter run by Carson Griffith, called "Rich People Sh — ."

Documents filed with the city show that JPMorgan's project is far from complete. Work on installing piping, drains and bathroom and kitchen fixtures appears to be ongoing, according to work permits filed earlier this month.

On a recent day, small crews were installing drywall in the building, with the entire structure draped in a tarp meant to re-create the building's facade. An open door to the site on Madison Avenue showed wires still hanging from the ceiling and dumpsters holding construction materials.

Renovating an old bank branch comes with its own complications. Last year, crews spent months disassembling the old branch's metal vault, piece by piece, said Paolo Alavian, owner of Altesi, an Italian restaurant next door.
